questions.question: Name the six factors that influence temperature and rainfall and explain briefly how each works.
questions.expected_answer: Latitude: near the equator the midday sun is high so energy is concentrated and temperatures are high; towards the poles the sun is lower, energy is spread out and temperatures fall; latitude also places a region within the pressure belts. Pressure belts and winds: rising air at the equatorial low brings convectional rain, sinking air at the subtropical highs brings dry weather, westerlies and cold fronts bring rain to the middle latitudes, and the belts shift with the seasons. Distance from the sea: water heats and cools slowly, so coasts are mild and interiors have a large range and are often drier. Altitude: temperature falls by about 6.5 degrees Celsius per 1 000 metres. Ocean currents: warm currents such as the Agulhas warm and moisten the air and bring rain; cold currents such as the Benguela cool and stabilise the air, bringing fog but little rain. Mountains: windward slopes receive relief rain, leeward slopes lie in a rain shadow.

questions.question: Explain the climate of the tropical rainforest, the savanna and the hot desert using the factors.
questions.expected_answer: Rainforest: near the equator the sun is high all year, so temperatures are about 25 to 28 degrees with a small range; the equatorial low pressure makes warm, moist air rise, cool and form convectional storms, giving more than about 2 000 mm of rain in every month. Savanna: at about 5 to 20 degrees, still hot; the rainy low-pressure belt moves over it in summer, giving a wet season, and moves away in winter, when subtropical high pressure brings a dry season, as in the Kruger Park. Hot desert: at about 15 to 35 degrees under the subtropical high pressure, where sinking air warms and dries so clouds rarely form; clear skies give very hot days and cold nights; cold currents such as the Benguela make west-coast deserts like the Namib drier, and distance from the sea adds to the dryness of the Kalahari.

questions.question: Explain why Cape Town has winter rain and why Johannesburg is cooler than its latitude suggests, using linked factor-process-effect chains.
questions.expected_answer: Cape Town: in winter the subtropical high-pressure belt moves north, so the westerly winds and cold fronts from the Southern Ocean reach the south-western Cape; moist air is forced to rise, partly by the Cape Fold Mountains, cools and condenses, forming rain. In summer the high pressure moves south over the Cape, so sinking air brings dry, sunny weather. Johannesburg: it lies at about 1 750 metres; temperature falls by about 6.5 degrees per 1 000 metres, so it is about 11 degrees cooler than a sea-level place at the same latitude; this explains its mild summers and frosty winter nights, with clear dry winter skies allowing heat to escape.
